ethiopia.title: Ethiopia's Abiy Inaugurates Major Megech Irrigation Dam
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia's Abiy Inaugurates Major Megech Irrigation Dam - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia's Abiy Inaugurates Major Megech Irrigation Dam 23 October 2026 Horn Diplomat (Hargeisa) By Kadir Moustapha Gondar — Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on Friday inaugurated the Megech Irrigation Dam Project in Gondar, a major infrastructure development aimed at expanding agricultural production, improving water supplies and creating economic opportunities for surrounding communities. The dam, with a storage capacity of 185 million cubic metres, is expected to irrigate more than 17,000 hectares of farmland, directly benefiting tens of thousands of farmers, Abiy said in a statement posted on X. "Today, we officially inaugurated the Megech Irrigation Dam Project, a major milestone for historic Gondar and its surrounding community," Abiy said. The prime minister said the project had faced years of delays and implementation challenges before the government resolved obstacles to its completion through its Medemer development philosophy. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Beyond agricultural irrigation, the dam is expected to provide reliable drinking water to Gondar and nearby towns, supporting efforts to improve access to essential services. Abiy said the artificial lake created by the dam would also support fisheries, urban agriculture and tourism development, potentially generating employment opportunities for young people and stimulating economic activity in the region. "The artificial lake will foster urban agriculture, large-scale fisheries, and tourism resorts, creating massive job opportunities for local youth," he said. The inauguration forms part of Ethiopia's broader efforts to expand irrigation infrastructure, improve agricultural productivity and strengthen water resource management. Abiy said sustained government monitoring had helped bring the long-delayed project to completion but acknowledged that Gondar required further development investment. "Gondar still deserves much more development. I urge the public to actively participate in its development," he said. The prime minister reaffirmed his government's commitment to ensuring that infrastructure investment and economic development benefit communities across Ethiopia. "We remain dedicated to ensuring Ethiopia's progress is inclusive, benefiting all regions and citizens," he added. Reporting by HornDiplomat News Desk) Read the original article on Horn Diplomat . ethiopia.summary: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed inaugurated the Megech Irrigation Dam Project in Gondar on October 23, 2026. This significant infrastructure initiative aims to enhance agricultural production, improve water supplies, and create economic opportunities for local communities. With a storage capacity of 185 million cubic meters, the dam is set to irrigate over 17,000 hectares of farmland, benefiting tens of thousands of farmers. Abiy highlighted that the project had faced numerous delays but was completed through the government's Medemer development philosophy. Beyond irrigation, the dam will provide reliable drinking water to Gondar and nearby towns, supporting essential services. The artificial lake created by the dam is also expected to promote urban agriculture, fisheries, and tourism, generating job opportunities for local youth. Abiy emphasized the need for further development investment in Gondar and reaffirmed the government's commitment to inclusive economic growth that benefits all regions and citizens of Ethiopia.

ethiopia.title: PM Abiy Stresses for Stronger Indigenous Capacity to Drive National Development
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: PM Abiy Stresses for Stronger Indigenous Capacity to Drive National Development - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: PM Abiy Stresses for Stronger Indigenous Capacity to Drive National Development 23 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has emphasized for stronger domestic institutional and human capacity, improved coordination among government institutions, and the removal of systemic bottlenecks to accelerate Ethiopia's development. Speaking at the inauguration of the Megech Irrigation and Water Supply Project in Gondar, the Prime Minister emphasized that sustainable national progress depends on strengthening local expertise and reducing reliance on external entities. Located on the Megech River, a major tributary of Lake Tana in the North Gondar Zone of the Amhara Region, the project is designed to expand agricultural production, improve access to clean drinking water and stimulate economic activity. With a storage capacity of 185 million cubic meters, the dam is expected to irrigate more than 17,000 hectares of farmland, benefiting tens of thousands of farmers. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn It will also provide a reliable supply of drinking water to Gondar and neighboring towns. Beyond irrigation and water supply, the project is expected to create additional economic opportunities through urban agriculture, fisheries and tourism development, generating employment for local youth and supporting the regional economy. Addressing the inauguration ceremony, PM Abiy stressed that building indigenous institutional and human capacity is essential to ensuring the effective implementation of development projects. He cited the 19-year delay in completing the Megech project as an example of structural weaknesses that have hindered the timely delivery of public infrastructure. He said the government had to replace the contractor and restructure the implementation process to bring the project to completion. The Prime Minister identified delays and the accumulation of unfinished projects as major obstacles to national development, emphasizing the need to address the underlying institutional and administrative challenges. He also underscored the importance of effective coordination between federal and regional governments, saying stronger collaboration and aligned implementation efforts are necessary to achieve shared development objectives. PM Abiy further emphasized that development infrastructure belongs to the public and requires collective responsibility for its protection and proper use. ethiopia.title: Kenya Red Cross Launches Emergency Response for Families Fleeing Moyale Clashes Into Marsabit
ethiopia.content: Kenya Red Cross Launches Emergency Response for Families Fleeing Moyale Clashes Into Marsabit - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Kenya Red Cross Launches Emergency Response for Families Fleeing Moyale Clashes Into Marsabit 23 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — The Kenya Red Cross Society (KRCS) has launched an emergency response for families arriving in Moyale, in Kenya's Marsabit County, after fleeing insecurity linked to renewed clashes across the border in Ethiopia, as fighting in the disputed border town has forced civilians to seek safety on the Kenyan side. "Our priority is to make sure every family arriving in Moyale is safe, sheltered and treated with dignity," KRCS Secretary General Dr. Ahmed Idris said in a statement, adding that the organisation's staff and volunteers would continue responding as humanitarian needs evolve. The initial response is intended to reach 1,000 households, with KRCS teams working alongside the Marsabit County Government, national authorities and humanitarian partners to establish temporary shelters and distribute tents and essential household supplies, including blankets, sleeping mats, jerrycans and kitchen sets. The organisation is also providing Super Cereal, a fortified porridge flour intended to support the nutritional needs of young children and pregnant and breastfeeding women, as well as first aid for people requiring immediate assistance. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn A rapid needs assessment is underway to identify priority requirements, with early findings pointing to urgent needs for food, safe water, sanitation and hygiene services, primary health care and protection, particularly for women, children, older people and persons with disabilities. KRCS is also helping separated family members reconnect. The response follows renewed violence in Moyale, where clashes between security forces from Ethiopia's Oromia and Somali regional states erupted on the morning of 22 October, following several days of escalating tensions over territorial and administrative disputes in the border town. The latest escalation followed a dispute over the opening of a Somali Regional State administrative office and the raising of its flag in Kebele 02, an area officials claim is administered by Oromia, a claim disputed by officials from the Somali region. The incident triggered an exchange of gunfire on 18 October, killing a 13-year-old girl, Diqqoo Jaataan Aagaa. Accounts differed over the circumstances of her death, with some attributing it to Somali regional forces and others saying she was caught in crossfire. Attempts by elders and security officials to defuse tensions, including an agreement to remove the flag, failed to secure a lasting resolution. Fighting subsequently spread to several localities in Moyale and parts of the wider East Borana Zone, while transport was disrupted, businesses closed and houses were reported burned. Addis Standard's reporting on the clashes documented civilian displacement, including women and children fleeing toward the Kenyan side of the border. Security officials on both sides confirmed casualties and injuries but did not disclose figures. The full scale of the displacement and humanitarian needs remained unclear. The latest developments echo an earlier cross-border displacement crisis in March 2018 , when Kenyan authorities and humanitarian organisations received thousands of Ethiopians fleeing violence in Moyale after Ethiopian army personnel killed civilians in the town. At the time, KRCS said it had received at least 2,000 Ethiopian asylum seekers in the Kenyan border town following their displacement. The organisation distributed emergency family kits containing tarpaulins, kitchen sets, mosquito nets, soap, thermal blankets and jerrycans, while the Marsabit County Government provided food assistance. A medical unit was also deployed as authorities and humanitarian partners assessed needs among the arrivals, most of whom were women and children. The current KRCS statement does not specify the number of people who have crossed into Kenya, identify the precise cause of the latest clashes beyond cross-border insecurity, or outline longer-term assistance plans. ethiopia.summary: The Kenya Red Cross Society (KRCS) has initiated an emergency response for families fleeing violence in Moyale, Marsabit County, due to renewed clashes across the border in Ethiopia. The conflict, which erupted on October 22, 2026, has forced civilians to seek refuge in Kenya. KRCS aims to assist 1,000 households by providing temporary shelters, tents, and essential supplies such as blankets, sleeping mats, and kitchen sets. Additionally, they are distributing Super Cereal, a fortified porridge, to support the nutritional needs of vulnerable groups, including young children and pregnant women. A rapid needs assessment is currently underway, revealing urgent requirements for food, clean water, sanitation, and healthcare, particularly for women, children, and the elderly. The clashes stem from territorial disputes between Ethiopia's Oromia and Somali regions, exacerbated by the raising of a Somali regional flag in a contested area. The situation has led to significant civilian displacement, echoing past crises in the region.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia's Abiy Unveils Ambitious Nuclear Energy Vision
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia's Abiy Unveils Ambitious Nuclear Energy Vision - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia's Abiy Unveils Ambitious Nuclear Energy Vision 22 October 2026 Horn Diplomat (Hargeisa) By Kadir Moustapha Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, Oct. 22, 2026 (Horndiplomat) — Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed visited the Ethiopian Nuclear Energy Commission to review progress in developing the country's nuclear energy programme, highlighting the role of advanced technology in Ethiopia's long-term economic transformation. During the visit, Abiy said Ethiopia must move beyond meeting its immediate economic needs and invest in scientific and technological development that would benefit future generations. "Ethiopia's next chapter is about transforming its immense potential and abundant natural resources into tangible development, technological advancement, and shared prosperity," Abiy said in a social media post following the visit. The prime minister stressed that reliable and sustainable energy was essential to industrialisation, manufacturing, digital infrastructure and broader economic development. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines He said nuclear technology offered Ethiopia an opportunity to strengthen its energy security while supporting scientific progress across several sectors. Beyond electricity generation, Abiy highlighted the potential applications of nuclear technology in healthcare, agriculture, industry and environmental protection, describing these fields as important areas for innovation and sustainable development. The Ethiopian Nuclear Energy Commission is responsible for establishing the institutional and technical foundations of the country's national nuclear energy programme. Abiy emphasised the importance of developing skilled professionals, strengthening scientific research and transferring technical knowledge to future generations. During the visit, the prime minister also spoke about Ethiopia's broader development ambitions, saying the country had a responsibility to lay the foundations for the advancement of Ethiopian civilisation. He said national development should not be limited to addressing immediate needs but should also focus on creating a lasting legacy for future generations across all sectors. The prime minister underscored the importance of ensuring that nuclear energy development proceeds peacefully, safely, responsibly and sustainably. Ethiopia's government views nuclear technology as part of its long-term efforts to expand energy capacity, strengthen scientific institutions and support economic transformation. During his visit, Abiy articulated the need for Ethiopia to invest in scientific and technological advancements that would benefit future generations, stating that the nation must leverage its natural resources for sustainable development. He highlighted the critical role of reliable energy in fostering industrialization, manufacturing, and digital infrastructure. Abiy also pointed out the diverse applications of nuclear technology beyond electricity generation, including healthcare, agriculture, and environmental protection. He underscored the importance of developing skilled professionals and enhancing scientific research to ensure the peaceful and responsible advancement of nuclear energy. The Ethiopian government views nuclear technology as a vital component of its long-term strategy to expand energy capacity and support economic growth, aiming to create a lasting legacy for future generations.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Records Tangible Progress in Building Sustainable, Healthy Food System
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Records Tangible Progress in Building Sustainable, Healthy Food System - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Records Tangible Progress in Building Sustainable, Healthy Food System 22 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia is transforming its agricultural sector to deliver affordable, healthy food, create jobs and protect natural resources, Ethiopian Agricultural Transformation Institute (ATI) Director General Mandefro Nigussie said. The 2026 World Food Day was celebrated in Addis Ababa under the theme "Innovate Today. Nourish Tomorrow," organized by the Ministry of Agriculture, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the World Food Program (WFP). The event was attended by government officials, members of the diplomatic community, development partners, researchers, farmers, pastoralists, youth and agricultural innovators. Addressing the occasion, Director General of ATI Mandefro Nigussie noted that the agricultural sector's contribution to the national economy remains high. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn He stated that Ethiopia is working with the main priority on accelerating the transfer of technology and innovation within the agricultural sector, further explaining that key emphasis has been placed on expanding irrigation and accelerating agricultural mechanization through policy, program, and institutional reforms. Furthermore, he added that significant investments are being carried out toward improving market systems and building a sustainable rural economy. He highlighted that indigenous knowledge of farmers and pastoralists has been integrated to implement climate-smart agricultural practices. Moving forward, he emphasized that collaboration among the government, regional states, researchers, and development partners is crucial to realizing the transformation of the food system. Workicho Jateno, Assistant Representative for the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) in Ethiopia, commended the tangible efforts of the Ethiopian government to ensure food security, boost the economy and reduce poverty. He reaffirmed that FAO will strengthen its partnership with Ethiopia and fully implement its country program framework running through 2030. The World Food Program (WFP) Country Director for Ethiopia Zlatan Milišić for his part praised Ethiopia's effective achievements in leveraging its youth potential, natural resources, and indigenous knowledge to transform its food system. The national strategies and policies established by the government in the sector have laid a strong foundation for these efforts, he noted. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia is making significant strides in transforming its agricultural sector to ensure sustainable and healthy food systems, as highlighted during the 2026 World Food Day celebrations in Addis Ababa. The event, themed "Innovate Today. Nourish Tomorrow," was organized by the Ministry of Agriculture, FAO, and WFP, and attended by various stakeholders, including government officials and farmers. Mandefro Nigussie, Director General of the Ethiopian Agricultural Transformation Institute (ATI), emphasized the sector's vital role in the national economy and the importance of technology transfer, irrigation expansion, and agricultural mechanization. Investments are being directed towards enhancing market systems and fostering a sustainable rural economy, integrating indigenous knowledge for climate-smart practices. FAO's Workicho Jateno and WFP's Zlatan Milišić praised Ethiopia's efforts in food security and economic growth, underscoring the need for continued collaboration among government, researchers, and development partners to sustain progress and leverage the country's resources effectively. This collective effort aims to secure a resilient food system for the future.

ethiopia.title: Fighting in Border Town Moyale Spreads to Three More Districts, Exchange of Heavy Gunfire
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Fighting in Border Town Moyale Spreads to Three More Districts, Exchange of Heavy Gunfire - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Fighting in Border Town Moyale Spreads to Three More Districts, Exchange of Heavy Gunfire 22 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — What started as a dispute over the raising of a Somali Regional State flag in Moyale town, Borana Zone, Oromia Region, followed by the killing of a 13-year-old girl on October 18, has escalated into sustained fighting, with security forces from the Oromia and Somali regions exchanging heavy gunfire. Tensions that had been building since Wednesday night erupted into open clashes on Thursday and spread to parts of Gumi Eldallo, Wachile, and Arero districts in South Oromia, residents and local security officials told Addis Standard . Moyale town residents told Addis Standard that fighting broke out at dawn on Thursday, around 5:30 a.m., in several locations, including Malab, Chamuk, Bole, Kebele 01, and Waqo Dogo localities. South Oromia security officials confirmed that the fighting later spread to parts of the East Borana Zone, including Melka Guba kebele in Gumi Eldallo District, Melka Adi and Melka Chophi kebeles in Wachile District, and an area known as Ela Orbi in Arero District. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn A resident of Moyale, Waqo Hussein, claims attempts by Somali Regional State special forces to raise a flag, along with the killing of 13-year-old Diqqoo Jaataan Aagaa and unverified rumors of assassination attempt against a city official on Tuesday evening as factors that contributed to the escalation. Regarding Thursday's fighting, Waqo said, "We took measures to defend and protect ourselves." A Moyale town official on the Oromia side also said that fighting broke out at dawn in several locations, claiming it as "a war declared on our people early in the morning by forces who have recently been making various provocations." A Somali resident of Moyale who fled with his family to the Ilu area of Moyale, Kenya, rejected the allegations from the Oromia side but confirmed that the flag dispute was central to the conflict. "This morning, October 22, it was forces from the Borana side who opened fire on us; they prevented us from raising our flag," he said. He further alleged that after the fighting began, forces from the Borana side burned houses belonging to Somali (Garre community) residents, along with offices and various signboards. Another Moyale resident from the Chamuk area told Addis Standard that government-backed Somali Regional forces equipped with heavy weaponry had attacked them. He said residents had identified the alleged attackers through identity cards recovered from deceased combatants and military communication equipment. Security officials from both sides confirmed casualties and injuries resulting from the fighting. However, while both side claim being provoked, neither side disclosed exact figures for those killed or wounded, citing the need to maintain operational secrecy. Residents on both sides said the fighting, which began around 5:30 a.m., appeared to ease around lunchtime but continued as of the time this report was compiled. Fighting spreads to other districts Residents and officials confirmed that the clashes spread to the East Borana Zone in the afternoon, intensifying in Melka Guba kebele in Gumi Eldallo District, Melka Adi and Melka Chophi kebeles in Wachile District, and Ela Orbi in Arero District. Transport movement in Moyale has come to a complete halt amid the fighting. Dozens of civilians, particularly women and children, have fled the town, while eyewitnesses and residents from both sides reported that numerous houses had been burned. Eyewitnesses who spoke to Addis Standard also said that, as of the time this report was compiled, neither the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) nor the Federal Police had intervened in the ongoing conflict. The latest fighting follows days of escalating tensions in Moyale after 13-year-old Diqqoo Jaataan Aagaa was killed in an exchange of gunfire on 18 October, amid a dispute over the opening of a new Somali Regional State administration office and the raising of its flag. The killing triggered protests, the closure of businesses, and disruptions to transport services as community elders and security officials discussed removing the flag. The dispute has since escalated into wider violence, with residents reporting casualties, property destruction, and displacement. Moyale, a flashpoint town administratively shared by Oromia and Somali regions, where areas under the two regional administrations are separated in places by a single lane, has repeatedly experienced clashes linked to territorial disputes between Borana communities in Oromia and Garre communities in the Somali Region. The clashes have resulted in deaths, displacement, and the burning of residents' homes. Tensions intensified in July and August 2025 after the Somali Regional State approved an administrative restructuring plan creating new woredas and zonal administrations. The move drew protests and criticism from Oromo opposition parties over changes affecting contested territories. Subsequent clashes along the Oromia-Somali border killed residents and displaced more than 288,000 people. Read the original article on Addis Standard . ethiopia.summary: Fighting in the border town of Moyale, Ethiopia, has escalated from a local dispute over the Somali Regional State flag to widespread violence affecting three additional districts: Gumi Eldallo, Wachile, and Arero. The conflict began on October 18, following the killing of a 13-year-old girl, which heightened tensions between security forces from the Oromia and Somali regions. Clashes erupted early on October 22, with reports of heavy gunfire and significant property damage, including the burning of homes. Residents have fled the area, and transport services have been disrupted. Both sides accuse each other of provocation, with claims of attacks and retaliatory violence. Eyewitnesses noted that the Ethiopian National Defense Force and Federal Police have not intervened. The ongoing violence reflects deeper territorial disputes between the Borana and Garre communities, exacerbated by administrative changes in the Somali Region that have previously led to significant unrest and displacement. The situation remains volatile, with casualties reported but unverified.

ethiopia.title: Peace Over Rivalry - Somalia's Future Lies in Cooperation, Not Confrontation With Ethiopia
ethiopia.content: Somalia: Peace Over Rivalry - Somalia's Future Lies in Cooperation, Not Confrontation With Ethiopia - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Somalia: Peace Over Rivalry - Somalia's Future Lies in Cooperation, Not Confrontation With Ethiopia 22 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Somalia needs a foreign policy that gives its people a better chance of living in peace. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud should place cooperation with Ethiopia at the center of that effort while protecting Somalia's sovereignty and maintaining its wider international partnerships. With so much unfinished work at home, Mogadishu cannot afford to let other governments' rivalries determine its relationship with its largest neighbor. The stakes are felt most clearly along a shared border stretching more than 1,500 kilometers. For pastoral families, traders, and communities connected by kinship, relations between the two countries are part of everyday life. A diplomatic rupture can mean a closed market, a disrupted journey, or greater insecurity. Those consequences deserve more weight in foreign policy than the visibility of a regional summit. Somalia has every right to build relations with Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan, and other partners. But each partnership should be judged by what it contributes to Somali security and recovery. Where another government's interests diverge from Somalia's, President Hassan Sheikh must preserve the freedom to choose his country's own course. Closer regional alignment becomes a liability if it draws Mogadishu into disputes with Addis Ababa that it has little ability to resolve or control. Moving beyond historical mistrust Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines This argument requires an honest account of history. Somali mistrust of Ethiopia did not emerge without reason. Under the EPRDF/TPLF-led government, military intervention and influence over Somali political actors left deep resentment. The 2006 intervention, when Ethiopian forces supported the Transitional Federal Government against the Islamic Courts Union, remains a powerful part of that memory. Cooperation will be difficult to sustain if those experiences are dismissed. As a former member of Ethiopia's House of Peoples' Representatives, I believe the region's leaders must take historical grievances seriously without allowing them to decide every future relationship. Communities on both sides of the border need governments willing to acknowledge past harm and negotiate a more dependable partnership. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's arrival in office in 2018 opened the way for a more constructive relationship with Somalia. Although Ethiopian troops continued operating in the country, the change in leadership offered an opportunity to move beyond the political interference associated with the previous administration. The task now is to consolidate that progress through security cooperation agreed with Somali authorities, respect for Somali institutions, and consistent restraint in Somalia's domestic political affairs. Mogadishu cannot afford to let other governments' rivalries determine its relationship with its largest neighbor." That responsibility is reciprocal. Ethiopia must respect Somalia's sovereignty, including in any negotiations over maritime access. Somalia should ensure that its territory and foreign partnerships do not support efforts to destabilize Ethiopia. Both governments have a legitimate interest in their neighbor's security, but neither should seek to determine the other's political future. Somali leadership, shared security The place of Ethiopian Somalis in national leadership also deserves attention. Ahmed Shide's election as Speaker of the House of Peoples' Representatives , Adem Farah's responsibilities as Vice President of the Prosperity Party and a federal official with Deputy Prime Minister rank, and Sultan Wolle's appointment as Minister of Irrigation and Lowlands place Somali leaders in positions of substantial national responsibility. In my view, these appointments reflect confidence in Somali leaders' contribution to Ethiopia's public life. Their importance is especially clear against a history in which the Somali region of Ethiopia was too often viewed through the concerns of security agencies. Representation is a right of citizenship, and its value must ultimately be measured by accountability and improvements in people's lives. Even so, the presence of Somali leaders in senior institutions is a meaningful part of contemporary Ethiopia that should inform a balanced assessment in Mogadishu. The two countries also share a security challenge that political disagreement cannot remove. Ethiopian forces formally joined the African Union Mission in Somalia in 2014 and have contributed to operations against al-Shabaab. Somalia has acknowledged the sacrifices of Ethiopian soldiers serving within African Union missions. That contribution merits recognition, alongside an insistence that all security arrangements respect Somali authority. The practical question is how to protect cooperation while Somalia strengthens its own institutions and assumes greater responsibility for national security. Mutual suspicion makes that task harder. When neighboring governments lose trust, armed groups gain room to exploit gaps in coordination. Neither country benefits from a relationship that leaves border communities more exposed. Case for practical cooperation President Hassan Sheikh could draw a useful lesson from President Ismail Omar Guelleh's engagement with Ethiopia. Djibouti has given its relationship with Addis Abeba a durable economic foundation through ports, transport corridors, and trade. These interests create reasons to keep talking when politics become difficult. Somalia can pursue a similarly practical approach, shaped by its own circumstances and priorities. The Ankara Declaration provides a basis for negotiated Ethiopian commercial access to the sea under Somalia's sovereign authority. Such arrangements would require clear terms, transparency, and safeguards for Somalia's long-term interests. Ethiopia, in turn, must pursue access through consent. If those conditions are met, port services and transport links could bring revenue and employment to Somalia while serving Ethiopian commerce. A functioning corridor can connect producers to markets and give businesses a reason to invest. Building those connections would give both governments something valuable to protect when disagreements arise. President Hassan Sheikh should keep direct dialogue with Addis Abeba open and make clear that Somalia's partnerships serve its reconstruction and security. Prime Minister Abiy should strengthen that confidence through respect for Somali sovereignty and consistent restraint in Somali domestic affairs. Neither leader needs to agree with every policy of the other to recognize the value of a stable relationship. Somalia's people have paid dearly for prolonged conflict. They deserve diplomacy that reduces the burdens on their recovery. A constructive relationship with Ethiopia will not settle every disagreement, but it can help make the neighborhood safer and create opportunities that confrontation would put at risk. President Hassan Sheikh has good reason to choose that course. ethiopia.summary: Somalia's future hinges on fostering cooperation with Ethiopia rather than succumbing to historical rivalries, according to President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud. Emphasizing the need for a foreign policy centered on collaboration, he argues that Somalia must prioritize its sovereignty while engaging with its largest neighbor. The extensive shared border impacts daily life for many, making diplomatic relations crucial for trade and security. Historical grievances stemming from Ethiopia's past interventions complicate this relationship, yet both nations must acknowledge these issues to build a stable partnership. The appointment of Somali leaders in Ethiopian governance reflects a growing integration that could enhance cooperation. Somalia's leadership should draw lessons from Djibouti's successful engagement with Ethiopia, focusing on economic ties that can withstand political tensions. By ensuring that partnerships contribute to Somalia's security and recovery, President Hassan Sheikh can navigate the complexities of regional dynamics while fostering a constructive relationship with Ethiopia. Ultimately, peace and collaboration can create opportunities for both nations and their citizens.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia's Coffee Sector Faces $453 Million Export Risk Under EU Deforestation Rules
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia's Coffee Sector Faces $453 Million Export Risk Under EU Deforestation Rules - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia's Coffee Sector Faces $453 Million Export Risk Under EU Deforestation Rules 22 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Ethiopia could lose up to $453 million in coffee export revenue under the European Union's deforestation regulation, with compliance gaps threatening to exclude smallholder farmers from a market that accounts for around 30% of the country's coffee exports, according to an October 2026 briefing paper by ODI Global. The study, The case of EUDR in Ethiopia : How to secure climate, trade and development goals, and overcome risks of market exclusion, warns that difficulties in tracing coffee to individual farms, documenting land-use legality and collecting plot-level geolocation data could expose up to 60% of smallholders to exclusion from EU-bound supply chains. The resulting disruption could reduce Ethiopia's gross domestic product by up to 0.5%, deepen foreign exchange shortages and transmit financial pressures through rural lending networks. The findings highlight a central challenge for Ethiopia as the EU prepares to enforce its Deforestation Regulation (EUDR): whether a policy designed to prevent forest loss can achieve its environmental objectives without imposing disproportionate costs on smallholder producers in developing countries. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Compliance gaps threaten smallholder access Ethiopia's coffee industry is particularly exposed because production is dominated by smallholders cultivating fragmented plots, many of which are less than one hectare. Around four million smallholder farmers account for approximately 95% of national coffee output, while the sector supports an estimated 15 million people across the value chain. The EUDR requires companies placing covered commodities on the EU market to demonstrate that products are deforestation-free and comply with relevant laws in their country of production. For coffee, this includes providing geolocation data linking shipments to the plots where the beans were grown. However, the ODI study identifies significant gaps in Ethiopia's preparedness. By July 2024, geolocation data had been compiled for approximately 200,000 hectares out of an estimated 860,000 hectares of coffee-growing land, equivalent to around 23%. Traceability presents another major obstacle. An estimated 57.4% of marketed coffee passes through local collectors or channels outside legally designated marketplaces, complicating efforts to track beans from individual farms through processing and export. The study estimates that geolocation constraints alone could put 10%-20% of smallholders at risk of exclusion, while traceability gaps could affect up to 57% of supply chains. Together with unresolved legal documentation requirements, these weaknesses could expose a substantially larger share of producers to exclusion. The consequences are already visible in parts of the sector. The Sidama Coffee Farmers' Cooperative Union told researchers that it had excluded 40% of its member cooperatives from EU exports because of compliance constraints. Meanwhile, the Oromia Coffee Farmers' Cooperative Union had collected geolocation data for only 92,000 of its more than 557,000 member farmers. Export losses could deepen economic pressures The potential losses extend beyond coffee-producing communities. According to ODI Global, Ethiopia could forfeit approximately $160 million in EU-destined coffee revenue under a scenario involving 20% exclusion, rising to $453 million if exclusion reaches 57%. These figures represent estimated gross export revenue losses, not necessarily the amount Ethiopia would ultimately lose after redirecting coffee to other markets. The study estimates that even if all excluded coffee could be sold elsewhere, lower prices in alternative markets could leave Ethiopia with net revenue losses ranging from approximately $42 million to $118 million. This distinction matters because Ethiopia has been expanding its coffee exports beyond Europe. The study notes that Asia accounted for approximately half of the country's coffee exports, compared with 28% for Europe and 12% for the United States. Yet EU-bound coffee often commands higher prices, making alternative destinations an imperfect substitute. The broader economic exposure is significant. Coffee accounts for approximately 35% of Ethiopia's merchandise export earnings, meaning EU-bound coffee represents an important source of foreign currency. ODI estimates that disruption to these exports could reduce foreign exchange earnings by between 2.2% and 6.3%, potentially reaching 8.5% under a severe scenario involving traceability and geolocation failures. Such a shock would compound existing pressures on foreign exchange availability, inflation and import costs. The study also warns that financial risks could spread through exporters, processors, cooperatives and banks that depend on coffee sales to service loans and finance seasonal procurement. Cooperative Bank of Oromia is particularly exposed because approximately 20%-30% of its loan portfolio is linked to coffee export financing, according to the study. Environmental objectives and local realities The study questions whether excluding Ethiopian smallholders would necessarily advance the regulation's environmental objectives. While deforestation remains a concern in Ethiopia, the researchers argue that coffee has not been a major driver of recent forest loss. Citing European Forest Institute data, the paper notes that no more than 20 coffee plots were linked to post-2020 deforestation. Ethiopia's coffee production systems frequently incorporate shade trees and forest cover. Garden coffee accounts for approximately half of national production, while semi-forest and forest systems contribute around 35% and 10%, respectively. The researchers warn that excluding farmers from higher-value European supply chains could weaken incentives to maintain these systems. Producers unable to meet compliance requirements may redirect their coffee to less-regulated markets or turn to alternative cash crops that could create greater pressure for land conversion. The paper therefore argues that compliance measures should be accompanied by incentives that reward sustainable production, including price premiums, carbon credits and payments for ecosystem services. Market diversification offers only partial relief Ethiopia has previously sought additional time to prepare for the regulation. In October 2024, the government welcomed the European Council's decision to postpone implementation by one year , following concerns over the costs and feasibility of meeting the original deadline. Addis Standard reported in April 2025, citing The New York Times , that Ethiopian coffee growers were struggling to meet the regulation's traceability requirements. Dejene Dadi, head of the Oromia Coffee Farmers' Cooperative Union, said the process was costly and difficult without additional support. The ODI study indicates that these concerns remain unresolved despite government efforts to establish national traceability systems and expand farm-level data collection. The Ethiopian Coffee Traceability Management System is intended to track coffee from production plots through processing and export. However, the researchers say its effectiveness remains uncertain while data collection, land registration and integration across supply-chain actors remain incomplete. Exporters have also indicated a willingness to redirect shipments to markets including China, the United States and Canada if European buyers do not help cover compliance costs. China's growing importance could provide additional opportunities. As Addis Standard previously reported, China had become Ethiopia's fourth-largest coffee importer, with exports reaching approximately 9,470 tonnes and generating $65.49 million during the first quarter of the 2025/26 fiscal year, according to the Ethiopian Coffee and Tea Authority. However, the ODI analysis suggests that diversification alone may not offset the loss of European price premiums. The study recommends that Ethiopia engage with EU authorities to clarify acceptable evidence of legal compliance, explore greater flexibility in applying the regulation and support smallholders and informal collectors in meeting traceability requirements. It also calls for stronger cooperative financing and transparent mechanisms to ensure that sustainability premiums reach producers. The regulation's implementation deadlines are approaching, with the study identifying late 2026 for large operators and mid-2027 for smaller enterprises under the phased timetable it examines. For Ethiopia, the challenge is therefore not simply to find new buyers. It is to preserve access to a valuable export market while ensuring that the costs of demonstrating environmental compliance do not undermine the livelihoods of the smallholders whose production systems the regulation is intended to protect. A report by ODI Global highlights that compliance challenges could exclude smallholder farmers, who produce about 95% of the country's coffee, from EU markets, which account for roughly 30% of Ethiopia's coffee exports. The study indicates that difficulties in tracing coffee to individual farms and collecting necessary geolocation data could put up to 60% of smallholders at risk of exclusion. This disruption could reduce Ethiopia's GDP by up to 0.5% and exacerbate foreign exchange shortages. The EUDR requires proof that coffee is deforestation-free, but Ethiopia's current traceability systems are inadequate. The report warns that excluding smallholders may not effectively address deforestation, as coffee production often incorporates sustainable practices. The Ethiopian government is urged to engage with EU authorities to clarify compliance requirements and support smallholders in meeting these challenges.

ethiopia.title: Drone Strikes Kill Schoolchildren in Amhara, Civilians in Tigray Regions As Conflicts Show No Sign of Abating
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Drone Strikes Kill Schoolchildren in Amhara, Civilians in Tigray Regions As Conflicts Show No Sign of Abating - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Drone Strikes Kill Schoolchildren in Amhara, Civilians in Tigray Regions As Conflicts Show No Sign of Abating Deutsche Welle A map of Ethiopia, showing the regional states of Tigray, Amhara and Afar. 22 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Drone strikes in Ethiopia's Amhara and Tigray regions killed schoolchildren and other civilians on Tuesday, 20 October, according to eyewitnesses and local residents who spoke to Addis Standard , adding to mounting civilian casualties amid renewed fighting between federal forces and armed opponents in both regions. In South Gondar Zone of Amhara, a drone strike hit Sana Elementary School in Dera Woreda, killing at least six schoolchildren and injuring more than 20 others, according to preliminary reports. Separately, a drone strike in Finaruo village, in Saharti Samre Woreda of Tigray's Southeastern Zone, killed four people and injured six others as they loaded livestock onto a truck, local residents said. The strikes occurred as drone attacks increasingly affect civilian areas and infrastructure in both regions, raising fresh concerns about civilian protection amid expanding aerial warfare. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines In Amhara, the strike on Sana Elementary School occurred between 10:00 and 11:00 a.m. on Tuesday, 20 October, in Sana Kebele, according to preliminary accounts. The injured children were taken to a local clinic, although their conditions were not immediately known. Casualty figures remain uncertain. While initial reports put the death toll at six, other accounts circulating publicly have reported between seven and ten students killed and more than 25 wounded. Addis Standard could not independently verify the total number of fatalities. An elementary schoolteacher who spoke to Addis Standard disputed claims circulating on social media that the strike targeted a nearby hideout used by Fano armed groups. "This was a school with more than 150 students attending the morning shift; there was no armed people in the school or nearby," the teacher said. "There was not conflict in nearby areas. Many of our students came back to school after three- or two-years interruptions. We don't know why the school was targeted." The teacher said more than 20 students had been wounded and that parts of two classrooms had been damaged, adding that the full extent of the destruction had yet to be assessed. Videos circulating on social media showed parents rushing into the school compound and carrying children away as pupils fled in different directions. Some children appeared disoriented, while teachers attempted to direct them to safety. Others could be heard calling for the wounded to be taken for medical treatment. Alemtshay, whose name has been changed for security reasons, told Addis Standard that her 11-year-old son, Dagim, had stayed home that morning because he was unwell. "He was having fever and was down with a terrible cold. I was pushing to go to school because he has already missed two years of school due to the war and school closures," she said. She recalled hearing screams from the neighborhood around 10:30 a.m., during the school's tea break, before families began rushing their injured children to a local clinic. "It was a complete chaos; mothers were crying and wailing," she said. "When we heard there was a bomb dropped from a helicopter, some men started to go around shouting for people to not leave their houses because they were afraid there might be another attack." Reflecting on her son's absence from school, she added: "I was unhappy when my son failed to go to the school but now, I know God was protecting him." In Tigray, the strike in Finaruo occurred at around 9:00 p.m. on Tuesday, 20 October, while a group of people were loading livestock onto an Isuzu truck, according to residents who spoke to Addis Standard . Four people were killed, including the livestock owner and three people assisting him, while an unspecified number of animals also died, the residents said. "What is most distressing is that the three of them were close relatives who were helping the owner," one resident told Addis Standard . The six injured people were taken to different hospitals for treatment. Three were admitted to Samre Hospital, while the other three, who sustained severe injuries, were taken to Ayder Comprehensive Specialized Hospital in Mekelle, according to the residents. Some of the wounded were aged between 13 and 17. One resident said there had been no military movements involving either federal forces or Tigrayan forces in the area in the days preceding the attack. "It has been almost days since the town was free of military movements from both sides," the resident said. The latest attack follows a series of drone strikes in Tigray that have killed and wounded civilians and damaged schools and humanitarian infrastructure. The attacks have continued amid renewed fighting between Ethiopian federal forces and Tigrayan forces, which intensified on 23 September. Earlier this month, a drone strike reportedly hit a shelter housing internally displaced people (IDPs) in Shiraro, in Tigray's Northwestern Zone, killing nine people and wounding 14 others, including a newborn baby. In Adwa, in the Central Zone, residents reported civilian deaths after drone strikes hit several locations in the city, although the exact toll could not be independently verified. Other reported drone attacks have damaged residential neighborhoods, hotels, schools and media facilities. In September, a drone strike destroyed a Catholic Relief Services truck carrying more than 41 metric tons of food assistance intended for an IDP camp in northwestern Tigray. The United States condemned the attack and called for a transparent public investigation. The renewed fighting follows the breakdown of the November 2022 Pretoria Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, which ended two years of devastating war in Tigray, and a sustained drone attacks . The latest escalation has displaced tens of thousands of people, with humanitarian organizations estimating that at least 150,000 people have been displaced across Tigray and neighboring Afar. In Amhara, federal forces have been fighting Fano armed groups since 2023, with drone strikes becoming a recurring feature of the conflict. Previous attacks reported by Addis Standard have hit residential areas , health facilities and religious sites, causing civilian casualties and damaging civilian infrastructure . The army has also targeted fighters on their own side killing at least 40 . In July this year, a drone strike on Saint Kirikos Monastery drew condemnation from the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and the World Council of Churches, which called for impartial investigations. Earlier attacks have also killed children and other civilians in residential communities across the region. The two latest strikes on Tuesday underscore the risks facing civilians as Ethiopia's conflicts increasingly involve aerial attacks by federal forces in populated areas. Addis Standard could not independently establish the circumstances of either strike, determine the intended targets or obtain an official response from the Ethiopian military. In Amhara, a drone strike targeted Sana Elementary School in Dera Woreda, killing at least six schoolchildren and injuring over 20 others. Eyewitnesses reported chaos as parents rushed to the school to help their injured children. A teacher disputed claims that the school was a target for armed groups, emphasizing the presence of students and the absence of conflict nearby. In Tigray, a separate drone strike in Finaruo village killed four people, including three relatives, while they were loading livestock. The strikes highlight the increasing impact of aerial warfare on civilian areas, raising concerns about safety and humanitarian conditions. The renewed fighting follows the collapse of a previous peace agreement, leading to significant civilian casualties and displacements across both regions. Humanitarian organizations estimate that at least 150,000 people have been displaced due to the ongoing violence.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia's Abiy Ahmed Honours Kenya's National Heroes
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia's Abiy Ahmed Honours Kenya's National Heroes - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia's Abiy Ahmed Honours Kenya's National Heroes 21 October 2026 Horn Diplomat (Hargeisa) By Kadir Moustapha Nairobi, Kenya — Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed paid tribute to Kenya's freedom fighters and national heroes during Mashujaa Day celebrations in Eldoret on Tuesday, highlighting the two countries' shared history of struggle, sacrifice and national unity. Speaking at the celebrations on October 20, Abiy praised the courage of Kenyans who fought for independence and those who sacrificed their lives to defend their country. The Ethiopian leader drew parallels between Kenya's struggle for freedom and Ethiopia's historic Battle of Adwa, when Ethiopian forces defeated an invading Italian army in 1896. "Kenya's history of courage and sacrifice resonates deeply with Ethiopia's own story of Adwa, where Ethiopians from every corner of the country united to defend their homeland," Abiy said in a statement posted on X. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn "These shared histories remind us that freedom was never given; it was won through courage, unity, and sacrifice." Abiy also called for stronger economic cooperation between Ethiopia and Kenya, identifying clean energy, regional connectivity, telecommunications and trade as key areas for expanding bilateral relations. "As our histories are intertwined, so too must our futures be," he said. "Through the spirit of Medemer, Ethiopia and Kenya must continue building on our existing cooperation in clean energy, connectivity, telecommunications, and trade to create greater opportunities and shared prosperity for our people." Medemer, a concept promoted by Abiy, emphasises unity, cooperation and collective efforts towards national development. Ethiopia and Kenya maintain close diplomatic and economic relations, with cooperation covering infrastructure development, electricity trade, regional security and cross-border connectivity. The two East African neighbours have also worked to strengthen regional economic integration through transport and energy infrastructure projects aimed at improving trade and investment opportunities. Mashujaa Day, celebrated annually on October 20, honours Kenyans who contributed to the country's independence and national development. Abiy concluded his remarks by saluting those recognised during the celebrations. "To all those honoured today, I salute you. Happy Mashujaa Day!" he said. Read the original article on Horn Diplomat . ethiopia.summary: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed honored Kenya's national heroes during the Mashujaa Day celebrations in Eldoret on October 20, 2026. His tribute emphasized the shared histories of struggle and sacrifice between Ethiopia and Kenya, particularly highlighting Kenya's fight for independence and the Ethiopian victory at the Battle of Adwa in 1896. Abiy praised the courage of Kenyans who defended their nation, stating, "These shared histories remind us that freedom was never given; it was won through courage, unity, and sacrifice." He called for enhanced economic cooperation between the two nations, focusing on clean energy, regional connectivity, telecommunications, and trade as vital areas for collaboration. Abiy's remarks underscored the concept of Medemer, which promotes unity and collective efforts for national development. The relationship between Ethiopia and Kenya is characterized by close diplomatic ties and joint initiatives in infrastructure and security. He concluded by saluting those honored during the celebrations, wishing them a happy Mashujaa Day.
